title: MACHINE LEARNING
body:
Machine learning is what you do when you cannot write the algorithm. Every other COMP course in
this degree teaches you to specify a procedure and prove things about it; here you specify a
*family* of procedures with free parameters, define a number that says how badly a given setting
of those parameters does, and let [[Optimization|optimisation]] pick the setting. The program is
not written, it is fitted. That single shift is why this course is downstream of the MATH block
rather than the COMP one: the interesting content is [[CALCULUS 1|calculus]],
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA|linear algebra]], and [[STATISTICS|statistics]] wearing new vocabulary.

The course runs on one worked example, a [[Neural Network]] trained by
[[Back Propagation]] on [[MNIST]], and takes the pieces of it in turn: what a
[[Neuron|neuron]] computes, why an [[Activation Function]] has to be there, what a
[[Loss Function]] measures, how [[Gradient Descent]] moves downhill on it, and how you tell
afterwards whether the thing works. The [[Information Theory]] block exists because the loss you
actually use for [[Classification|classification]] is [[Cross-Entropy Loss]], and that is an
information-theoretic quantity, not an arbitrary formula.

## Topics

### The learning problem

The setup every model in the course shares, and the vocabulary the rest of the file assumes.

- [[Classification]]: predict which of a finite set of labels an input belongs to. The course's
  default problem.
- [[Binary Classification]]: the two-label case, where the whole evaluation vocabulary below is
  defined and where a single probability is enough to specify the answer.
- [[Logistic Regression]]: the smallest honest classifier, a linear score squashed to a
  probability. Everything a network does, one layer deep.
- [[Linear Regression]] ([[STATISTICS]]): the smallest supervised model of all, and the one case
  where the fit has a closed form and no optimiser is needed.
- [[MNIST]]: the handwritten digit set the course's examples run on.
- [[Stratification]]: how you split data so the split does not lie to you.

**Model, loss, optimiser** is the decomposition to carry through the whole course. Every method in
the folder is a choice of the three, and they are independent choices:

| Piece | What it fixes | Examples in this vault |
|---|---|---|
| **Model** | the family of functions you are allowed to fit | [[Linear Regression]], [[Logistic Regression]], [[Multilayer Perceptron]], [[CNN]] |
| **Loss** | what "wrong" costs | squared error, [[Log Loss]], [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] |
| **Optimiser** | how you search the parameter space | closed form ([[Least Squares]]), [[Gradient Descent]], [[SGD Classification\|SGD]] |

### Network anatomy

What a network is made of, from the single unit up.

- [[Neuron]]: a [[Dot Product]] of inputs against [[Weights]], plus a [[Bias Term]], through an
  [[Activation Function]]. The entire unit.
- [[Perceptron]]: the single-layer original, and the note that carries what it *cannot* do.
- [[Multilayer Perceptron]]: perceptrons stacked, which is what "neural network" usually means.
- [[Neural Network]]: the index note for the whole structure.
- [[Input Layer]], [[Hidden Layer]], [[Output Layer]]: the three roles a layer can have.
- [[Weights]]: the learned parameters. The only thing training changes.
- [[Bias]] and [[Bias Term]]: the per-unit offset, and the two unrelated things "bias" means.
- [[Forward Pass]]: running the network, which *is* [[Matrix Multiplication]].
- [[CNN]]: the architecture that exploits the fact that images have spatial structure.
- [[Computer Vision]]: what CNNs were built for.

### Activation functions

The non-linearity, and the reason depth means anything at all.

- [[Activation Function]]: the general role, and how you pick one per layer.
- [[Non-Linear]]: the load-bearing property. Without it a deep network collapses to one layer.
- [[Sigmoid]]: squashes to $(0,1)$, so its output reads as a probability. Saturates.
- [[ReLU]]: $\max\{0, z\}$, the default hidden-layer choice, and why it beat the sigmoid.
- [[Leaky ReLU]]: the patch for ReLU's dead-unit failure.

### Training

How the parameters actually move. All three of these notes are the MATH block applied.

- [[Loss Function]]: the number being minimised, and why it must be differentiable.
- [[Log Loss]] and [[Cross-Entropy Loss]]: the classification losses, which are the same object.
- [[Gradient Descent]]: step downhill by the [[Gradient]], repeat. [[Optimization]] with too many
  variables to solve directly.
- [[SGD Classification]]: estimate the gradient from a minibatch instead of the whole dataset.
- [[Back Propagation]]: the [[Chain Rule]] applied through a composition of layers, computed
  backwards so the shared factors are reused.

### Evaluation

Whether the fitted thing works. This block is [[STATISTICS]] under different names, and
[[Type I and Type II Errors]] carries the translation.

- [[Confusion Matrix]]: the four cells, and the object all the rates below are computed from.
- [[True Positive]], [[True Negative]], [[False Positive]], [[False Negative]]: the cells.
- [[Sensitivity]]: caught positives, $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})$. Statistical power.
- [[Specificity]]: correctly cleared negatives, $\text{TN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FP})$.
- [[Stratification]]: preserve the class proportions when splitting, or the metrics are noise.

### Information theory

Why the classification loss has the shape it does.

- [[Information Theory]]: the framing, and $I(x) = -\log_2 P(x)$.
- [[Information]]: surprise. A certain event carries none.
- [[Entropy]] and [[Shannon Entropy]]: expected surprise, so the cost of the best possible code.
- [[Cross-Entropy]]: the cost of coding truth $P$ with your model $Q$.
- [[KL Divergence]]: the excess you pay for being wrong, the gap between the two above.

### The linear algebra underneath

Borrowed wholesale from [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]; linked, not restated.

- [[Principal Component Analysis]]: dimensionality reduction, and the vault's route from the MATH
  block into this course. The chain is [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] →
  [[Spectral Theorem]] → [[Singular Value Decomposition]] → PCA → here.
- [[Vector Norm]]: where regression losses come from. $L_2$ squared is mean squared error.
- [[Least Squares]]: the closed-form fit, and what gradient descent is the slow route to.
- [[NumPy]]: the array library all of this is written in.

## Core Facts to Know

- Machine learning is fitting parameters, not writing procedures. The three independent choices are
  **model, loss, optimiser**.
- A [[Neuron]] computes $\sigma(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b)$: a [[Dot Product]], a
  [[Bias Term]], an [[Activation Function]]. Nothing else.
- A [[Forward Pass]] **is** [[Matrix Multiplication]]. Stack a layer's [[Weights]] as a
  [[Matrix]], multiply the input [[Vector]], apply the activation, repeat.
- **Without a non-linear activation, depth buys nothing.** A composition of linear maps is a linear
  map, so an $n$-layer linear network has exactly the expressive power of one layer.
- [[Back Propagation]] is the [[Chain Rule]] and nothing else. It runs backwards because that order
  reuses factors already computed instead of recomputing them per weight.
- [[Gradient Descent]] exists because the closed form disappears. With one variable you set
  $f'(x) = 0$ and solve; with a million [[Weights]] you evaluate the derivative and step.
- Each gradient step is a [[Linear Approximation]] trusted for a short distance. The learning rate
  is choosing how far to trust it.
- [[SGD Classification|Stochastic]] gradient descent works because a minibatch gradient is an
  *unbiased* estimate of the true one, with standard error shrinking as $1/\sqrt{n}$.
- A loss must be differentiable, which is why **accuracy cannot be used as a loss**: it is flat
  almost everywhere and its gradient carries no information.
- $L_2$ squared residual = mean squared error, $L_1$ = mean absolute error. Both are
  [[Vector Norm|norms]]; [[Log Loss]] and [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] are not.
- [[Log Loss]] and [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] are **the same function**, named from the likelihood side
  and the information side respectively.
- $H(P) = -\sum P(x)\log P(x)$ is expected surprise. $H(P,Q) = -\sum P(x)\log Q(x)$ is the cost of
  using the wrong model. $D_{KL}(P\|Q) = H(P,Q) - H(P)$ is the excess, and it is never negative.
- Minimising [[Cross-Entropy]] over a fixed dataset is minimising [[KL Divergence]], because
  $H(P)$ does not depend on your parameters.
- A [[Confusion Matrix]] and a statistician's Type I / Type II table are **the same four cells**.
  [[False Positive]] is $\alpha$, [[False Negative]] is $\beta$, [[Sensitivity]] is power $1-\beta$.
- **Accuracy is useless on imbalanced data.** A classifier that always says "negative" scores 99% on
  a 1-in-100 problem. This is why [[Stratification]] and the per-cell rates exist.
- Moving the decision threshold trades [[Sensitivity]] against [[Specificity]]. It does not improve
  both; only more data does that.
- [[Principal Component Analysis]] is an eigendecomposition of a covariance matrix, so it is
  [[Variance]] and [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] and nothing new.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] (MATH 1200): **the course this one actually runs on.** [[Optimization]] owns the
  closed-form-versus-iterative distinction, [[Chain Rule]] owns backpropagation's mechanics, and
  [[Linear Approximation]] is what a gradient step *is*. None of that is re-derived here.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200): [[Gradient]] and [[Partial Derivative]] are what a
  derivative becomes with a million inputs, and [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] is the sum-over-paths
  version [[Back Propagation]] needs.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203): [[Matrix Multiplication]] is a forward pass, [[Dot Product]] is a
  neuron, [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] is the start of the PCA chain.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303): the keystone.
  [[Principal Component Analysis]], [[Vector Norm]], [[Least Squares]], and [[Image Processing]]
  all belong to it and are borrowed here.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): **the statistical floor under this folder.**
  [[Type I and Type II Errors]] owns the evaluation table, [[Random Variable]] and
  [[Probability Distribution]] own expectation, [[Bernoulli Distribution]] is what
  [[Logistic Regression]] fits, [[Sampling Distribution]] is why minibatches work, and
  [[Linear Regression]] is the simplest model there is.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] (`Books/`): the neural-network notes physically live there, since
  that is where Evan wrote them. Same material, different folder.
- [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]]: the broader field this is one method within, and **the division
  between the two folders is deliberate**. That course owns the *agent*: search
  ([[A* Search]], [[Heuristic]]), decisions under uncertainty ([[Rational Agent]],
  [[Expected Utility]]), and learning from consequences ([[Reinforcement Learning]],
  [[Q-Learning]]). This folder owns learning from data as a subject in its own right. It also
  owns the three models this one never wrote: [[Decision Tree]], [[Random Forest]], and
  [[Clustering]], which were logged here as content gaps until 2026-08-17.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: gradient descent is an optimisation algorithm and gets analysed
  the same way. [[Time Complexity]] applies to training as much as to sorting.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631): decision trees are a [[Tree]], and the
  [[Weighted Graph]] machinery is the same "edges carry numbers" idea a network runs on.
